claims.text: The FeNiCrCoCu coating on a Cu matrix has stable wear resistance at 300 K.
The coating has a high elastic modulus at 300 K.
The initial coating contains a pre-existing population of dislocations.
The initial coating contains stacking faults.
Increasing temperature under nanoindentation and friction causes a transition from stable to unstable wear behavior.
At a critical temperature, thermally activated lattice softening overcomes a stacking-fault energy barrier.
Crossing the critical temperature causes a rapid collapse in dislocation density.
Crossing the critical temperature shifts deformation from defect-mediated plasticity to homogeneous atomic disorder.
At low temperatures, dislocation pile-ups impede slip and help maintain wear resistance.
At low temperatures, stacking-fault barriers impede slip and help maintain wear resistance.
Rising temperature produces lattice softening that reduces the Peierls stress.
Rising temperature and lattice softening reduce the stacking-fault energy.
The temperature-induced changes in Peierls stress and stacking-fault energy promote dislocation annihilation.
The temperature-induced changes in Peierls stress and stacking-fault energy promote cross-slip.
At the critical temperature, the energy barrier for atomic disorder drops.
The lowered barrier for atomic disorder changes deformation from localized dislocation glide to rapid homogeneous lattice disordering.
Homogeneous lattice disordering eliminates the material's ability to sustain load-bearing defects.
The critical transition produces a sharp decline in wear resistance.
The critical transition produces a sharp decline in elastic modulus.
The onset of wear failure is accompanied by a measurable drop in dislocation density and loss of stacking-fault contrast.
